Finer grids (81–90 tiles) pay the most in quality loss, and more overlap beyond moderate levels buys nothing and degrades quality [S1, unofficial].

The claim is explicitly supported by the text in Source [S1]. The 'Source [S1] notes' section contains the exact sentence: 'Finer grids (81–90 tiles of a few hundred splats each) pay the most in quality loss. More overlap beyond moderate levels buys nothing and degrades quality.' Additionally, the 'Supplementary Document 11' passage confirms that 'the finest grids (81–90 tiles of a few hundred splats each) pay the most' and that 'more overlap buys nothing and 40% costs 0.54–1.68 dB', which supports the claim that excessive overlap degrades quality relative to moderate levels.

It is distinguished from non-overlapping tiling by the application of a raised-cosine (Hann) taper in overlap regions, which ensures a partition-of-unity and prevents visible seams, keeping the seam-to-interior residual ratio within 1.01–1.13 of a monolithic fit [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that the method is distinguished by applying a raised-cosine (Hann) taper in overlap regions to ensure a partition-of-unity and prevent visible seams. It further confirms that this approach keeps the seam-to-interior residual ratio within 1.01–1.13 of a monolithic (seamless) fit, whereas hard cuts or overlaps without taper result in significantly higher ratios.

The stride between tile origins is $T - L$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the stride between tile origins is $T - L$. In Source [S1], under the section describing 'Tiled fitting', it explicitly states: 'Luxar partitions the volume into overlapping tiles on a regular grid with stride T − L, where T is the tile size and L is the overlap.' This directly confirms the claim.

It solves the problem of GPU memory exhaustion for large volumes (e.g., $2048^3$ float32) by decomposing the domain into smaller, manageable chunks [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that a '2048^3 float32 volume that would exceed consumer GPU memory... could thus be decomposed into overlapping 256^3 tiles' to fit within memory constraints (e.g., 24 GB). This directly supports the claim that the method solves the problem of GPU memory exhaustion for large volumes by decomposing the domain into smaller chunks.

This window is applied along each overlap face [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that a window is applied along each overlap face. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the 'Tiled fitting' section, stating: 'Before fitting, each tile’s voxel data is multiplied by a raised-cosine (half-Hann) taper ... applied along each overlap face, producing a partition-of-unity'. This matches the claim exactly.
supported
*   **Strengths:** Enables fitting of volumes larger than GPU memory; seamless blending via partition-of-unity; scalable via parallel scheduling [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly supports all three components of the claim: 1) 'Enables fitting of volumes larger than GPU memory' is supported by the note that a 2048^3 volume is decomposed into smaller tiles to fit within consumer GPU memory (e.g., 24 GB). 2) 'Seamless blending via partition-of-unity' is supported by the description of applying raised-cosine (half-Hann) taper to ensure adjacent windows sum to 1.0 (partition-of-unity). 3) 'Scalable via parallel scheduling' is supported by the statement that tiles are 'embarrassingly parallel' and scheduling is built in via batch fitting across multiple GPUs or Slurm array jobs.
supported
*   Avoid hard cuts or overlap without tapering [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'overlapping tiles without taper are worse' and that 'hard cut without overlap raises near-seam error up to 50-fold' (or raises the seam-to-interior residual ratio significantly). It further details that applying a raised-cosine (half-Hann) taper ensures a partition-of-unity and keeps the error ratio low (1.01–1.13). Therefore, the evidence supports the claim that one should avoid hard cuts and overlap without tapering.

Fit the Gaussian splat model for each tile independently using the assigned seed count $N_i$ [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that for volumes exceeding GPU memory, the system partitions the volume into overlapping tiles and 'Each tile is fitted independently'. It further details that the integer seed budget is divided over these tiles (proportionally to their weighted voxel count and intensity), effectively assigning a specific seed count $N_i$ to each tile for independent fitting.
